chapters.body: Bell had not yet rung at Pasir Panjang English School, and a group of boys were already on the field kicking a football before afternoon session. Among them was Canagasabai Kunalan, born 23 October 1942. He had grown up in a big house in Johor, where his father worked as a medical officer. The family later came to Singapore and lived on Alexandra Road. He had three sisters, the eldest adopted by his father, and his father ran a clinic inside a brewery compound. On afternoon-session days he went early to play, though, as he later put it, "I was not good enough to play for the school so I just played for fun."

quote.text: I was not good enough to play for the school so I just played for fun.

chapters.title: Football before the bell
chapters.turn: Nothing about him yet suggested a runner.
chapters.voice: Nobody watching would have picked him out.

chapters.body: At secondary school he wandered down to the Sports Day trials on a whim, and the house master entered him in the One Mile Open. He had done no training, yet he finished third, and the following year he won the race. His O-level results were not good enough to continue studying, so his father sent him to night school, and afterwards he taught at Gillman Barracks. With little to fill his days, he played football up to three times a day. With other Indian boys he formed the Indian Youth Football Team. The running seemed to stop there.
chapters.title: The One Mile Open
chapters.turn: Teaching would soon bring an unexpected visitor.
chapters.voice: With no training, third. A year later, first.

chapters.body: He had become a teacher by chance and was posted to Tiong Bahru Primary School, where he taught in primary schools from 1961 to 1966. One day a colleague saw him playing football with his pupils and asked him to run a relay at the Teachers' Training College. The colleague told the coach, Olympian sprinter Tan Eng Yoon, who invited him to train at Farrer Park. Kunalan doubted he could ever be a sprinter and did not turn up for six months, until he bumped into Tan, who kept visiting Tiong Bahru Primary. As Kunalan recalled, Tan told him, "I can recognise potential when I see it." He did not know what potential meant. On the ninth visit he agreed to train.

quote.text: I can recognise potential when I see it.

chapters.title: Nine visits to Tiong Bahru
chapters.turn: He had no idea how fast things would move.
chapters.voice: He said no for six months, until the ninth visit.

chapters.body: He first took up running in 1963, aged 20. Training fitted around teaching, with endurance runs at MacRitchie Reservoir, strength work at a friend's house, and sessions under a tree at Farrer Park, where the weights were kept in the ladies' toilet. He later insisted, "We had all the basic equipment and facilities." After only five months of training he ran 10.9 seconds for 100 metres, 22.3 seconds for 200 metres and 50.9 seconds for 400 metres. Tan, then national coach, said he had shown the most improvement of any athlete. At the Malaysia Sports Festival in Kuala Lumpur he ran in a 4x100 metre relay team with Cedric Monteiro, Wong Fey Wan and Low Sin Chock that set a Singapore record of 42.0 seconds.

quote.text: We had all the basic equipment and facilities.

chapters.title: Weights in the ladies' toilet
chapters.turn: Then came a selection that pleased no one.
chapters.voice: Five months in, he was already setting records.

chapters.body: His selection for Malaysia's Olympic 4x100 metre relay angered sprinter Wong Fey Wan, who challenged him publicly in the press: "I am willing to race against Kunalan again to prove I am the better man over 100 m." Kunalan later called the affair one of the saddest moments of his career. He never knew if he had been picked on merit and wished Wong had gone instead. At the Tokyo Olympics he ran in Malaysia's 4x100 metre relay with Mani Jegathesan. Three days before his 22nd birthday the team finished last in its first-round heat.

quote.text: I am willing to race against Kunalan again to prove I am the better man over 100 m.

chapters.title: A place he never asked for
chapters.turn: Off the track, a different race was starting.
chapters.voice: He wished the other man had gone instead.

chapters.body: He met Chong Yoong Yin, Raffles Girls' School sprint champion and national sprinter, on the track in 1964. Both were 22, and friendship grew slowly into love. Their parents disapproved of an Indian-Chinese couple. As he left for a Wilson David concert with her, his parents gave him an ultimatum not to come back if he went out with her that day. He went upstairs, took his birth certificate and left home. "My eyes were almost tearing, and my hair was standing." A colleague put him up, and next day he rented a room from a pupil's mother for S$30 a month. Months later her father and uncle gave Chong the same ultimatum. She left and moved in with her estranged mother, who had left her father when Chong was 12.

quote.text: My eyes were almost tearing, and my hair was standing.

chapters.title: The birth certificate
chapters.turn: They would have to build their own circle.
chapters.voice: They had each other, and not much else.

chapters.body: Shunned by both families, he decided they would build their own circle with friends who would accept them. They got engaged in October 1965 and posted wedding invitations to family knowing they would not come. One Sunday morning his father knocked on the door and offered his blessing if Chong converted to Hinduism and took a Hindu name. Within two weeks she became Rajeshwari. She said she was a freethinker and did it to pacify everyone. His father's auspicious day was 17 April 1966, the very date they had picked. They held a Hindu ceremony at Sri Mariamman Temple in the morning, a S$4-a-head high tea at the Adelphi Hotel in the afternoon and, for her mother, a Chinese banquet at night. "We got married three times. That's probably how we have stayed married for almost 60 years now."

quote.text: We got married three times. That's probably how we have stayed married for almost 60 years now.

chapters.title: Married three times
chapters.turn: Bangkok waited, with a finish too close to see.
chapters.voice: Three ceremonies in one day to keep everyone together.

chapters.body: In Bangkok in December three men reached the finish of the 100 metres at the Asian Games together, and all were timed at 10.5 seconds. Kunalan took silver. Gold went to Jegathesan, by 0.01 seconds, his rival and friend Jega. Bronze went to Iijima. Three men shared one time. Kunalan also won bronze in the 4x400 metre relay. To lose gold by a hundredth of a second left him with silver and bronze from the same meeting. He had run level with Jegathesan and Iijima, and the hundredth of a second had decided it.
chapters.title: One hundredth of a second
chapters.turn: He would soon learn how near he was.

chapters.body: Until the last days before departure it was not clear he had the funds to travel to the Mexico City Olympics. In Mexico City he ran 10.38 seconds for the 100 metres, advancing past the first round. It stood as Singapore's national record for 33 years. US assistant coach Stan Wright let him use Team USA's masseurs. Bahamian sprinter Tom Robinson told him he was straining too hard in the first 20 metres. He then watched Beamon's leap and Fosbury's jump from the stands. In a letter to his wife he measured himself against the world's best: "Arms and legs big!! Mine only 1/2."

quote.text: Arms and legs big!! Mine only 1/2.

chapters.title: Arms and legs big
chapters.turn: Home brought more gold, then another hard stop.
chapters.voice: Through to the second round, and into the record books.

chapters.body: He was named Singapore's Sportsman of the Year in 1968 and again in 1969. At the 1969 SEAP Games he won three golds in the 100 metres, 200 metres and 4x400 metre relay. At the 1970 Asian Games a photo finish again denied him. Given the same time as two others, he was awarded bronze, and injury forced his first retirement at the end of 1970. He came back. On 1 September 1973, in an all-white track suit, he carried the flame into the new National Stadium and lit the SEAP Games cauldron at its highest point, the first person to do so. In 1975 he anchored Singapore's 4x400 metre relay to gold. Years later, at the old National Stadium's farewell, he led a V of Team Singapore athletes round the track and raced up the gallery steps to light its cauldron for the last time.
chapters.title: The flame at the top
chapters.turn: The track was ending; the classroom was waiting.
chapters.voice: The first to light it, and the last.

chapters.body: He taught for 13 years at Dunearn Secondary Technical School from 1967 to 1980. A heel injury, not age, ended his competitive career in 1979. In 1980 he joined the Institute of Education as a lecturer, later assistant professor, teaching functional anatomy, exercise physiology and conditioning. Scholarships took him to Perth in 1980, to West Germany in 1983-84 for a course taught in German, and to Loughborough for a master's. His students called him Mr K. His rule was to make track and field fun: "Don't let them hate T&F; don't let them hate you." Aged 39 he ran 400 metres in 48.8 seconds at the Swifts Club championships at the National Stadium. As national sprint coach from 1993 to 1996 he saw his sprinters break the 4x100 metre record in 1994, a record he had helped set in 1974.

quote.text: Don't let them hate T&F; don't let them hate you.

chapters.title: Mr K
chapters.turn: His own oldest record was about to fall.
chapters.voice: Records are made to be passed on.

chapters.body: In 2001 his 100 metre record fell, lowered by 0.01 seconds by U. K. Shyam, a sprinter he had mentored. On 11 January 2002 he was inducted into the Sports Hall of Fame at the Fullerton Hotel, and in his speech he singled out his wife. She had stopped competing when pregnant and raised their three daughters, making sure he ate enough protein. A brain-tumour operation later left her with a drooping eyelid and deaf in one ear. He left the National Institute of Education in June 2010 and in August, aged 67, joined the Singapore Sports Council looking after past Olympians. He retired from Sport Singapore in 2022 to spend more time with his wife, and kept running. Looking back on six decades together, he told Tabla in 2026, "As a couple, we must not feel that we want to be superior. We are equals."

quote.text: As a couple, we must not feel that we want to be superior. We are equals.

chapters.title: Still running
chapters.voice: He kept going, because she kept him going.

conflicts.choice: Book follows grew up in Johor and family later came to Singapore, with no date given.
Book follows colleague relay and Tan Eng Yoon nine visits to Tiong Bahru.
Book follows Tabla ultimatum before Wilson David concert.
Book follows first retirement end-1970, comeback, final retirement 1979.
Book follows joining Institute of Education around 1980.
Book follows 10.38 s advancing past first round to second round.
Book follows Chong Yoong Yin, keeping Yoong Ying spelling only inside quoted line.
